papers.conclusion: The shared task demonstrated that ensembling and regularization are promising directions for circuit discovery, and non-linear projections can improve causal variable localization, though more controls are needed to ensure learned features capture genuine model variables. The MIB leaderboard will continue to accept submissions to facilitate progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Ensembling strategies (parallel, sequential, hybrid) and regularization techniques (filtering unstable components) proved effective for circuit localization, achieving strong CPR and CMD scores.
Non-linear featurizers (using MLPs and activation functions) and orthogonal non-linear projections significantly improved causal variable localization over baseline methods like DAS.
The best method for circuit localization depended on the chosen metric (CPR vs. CMD), with no single method dominating across all tasks and models.
The shared task received a relatively small number of submissions, indicating room for broader community participation and method development.
The MIB leaderboard remains open for ongoing submissions, providing a standardized framework for future mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The shared task received a relatively small number of submissions, which may limit the generalizability of the findings.
For causal variable localization, non-linear featurizers are highly expressive and could learn features not actually present in the model, requiring additional validation to ensure they capture genuine causal variables.
future_direction: Continue exploring ensembling strategies and regularization techniques for circuit discovery.
Develop more expressive featurizer training formulations that leverage existing mediator types for causal variable localization, while ensuring proper controls to isolate concepts truly in the model.
Conduct detailed comparisons of methods on more fine-grained distributions to characterize when and why each method is likely to succeed, and compare compute requirements.
papers.abstract: Dana Arad, Yonatan Belinkov, Hanjie Chen, Najoung Kim, Hosein Mohebbi, Aaron Mueller, Gabriele Sarti, Martin Tutek. Proceedings of the 8th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP. 2025.

papers.title: Out of Order: How important is the sequential order of words in a sentence in Natural Language Understanding tasks?
papers.research_question: How important is the sequential order of words in a sentence for state-of-the-art natural language understanding models? Do BERT-based models use word order information when solving NLU tasks?
papers.core_contribution: BERT-based models are largely insensitive to word order in many GLUE tasks, relying on superficial cues like keyword sentiment or word overlap; increasing their sensitivity to word order through synthetic task finetuning improves performance on most GLUE tasks and SQuAD 2.0.
papers.conclusion: Many GLUE tasks do not challenge machines to understand the meaning of a sentence, as models rely on superficial cues and are largely insensitive to word order.
papers.key_findings:
75% to 90% of correct predictions of BERT-based classifiers on GLUE tasks remain constant after input words are randomly shuffled.
BERT-based models exploit superficial cues (e.g., sentiment of keywords, word-wise similarity between sequence-pair inputs) when tokens are shuffled.
The contribution of individual words to classification is almost unchanged even after surrounding words are shuffled (except for CoLA and RTE).
In SST-2, the polarity of a single salient word is ≥60% predictive of the sentence's label.
BERT-based models use a set of self-attention heads for finding similar tokens shared between two inputs in sequence-pair tasks.
Encouraging models to capture word order information improves performance on most GLUE tasks and SQuAD 2.0.
papers.abstract: Do state-of-the-art natural language understanding models care about word order? Not always! We found 75% to 90% of the correct predictions of BERT-based classifiers, trained on many GLUE tasks, remain constant after input words are randomly shuffled. Although BERT embeddings are famously contextual, the contribution of each individual word to classification is almost unchanged even after its surrounding words are shuffled. BERTbased models exploit superficial cues (e.g. the sentiment of keywords in sentiment analysis; or the word-wise similarity between sequencepair inputs in natural language inference) to make correct decisions when tokens are randomly shuffled. Encouraging models to capture word order information improves the performance on most GLUE tasks and SQuAD 2.0. Our work suggests that many GLUE tasks are not challenging machines to understand the meaning of a sentence.

papers.title: Do Language Models Associate Sound with Meaning? A Multimodal Study of Sound Symbolism
papers.research_question: How do Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) associate sound-symbolic words with semantic features similar to human phonetic intuition, and how do their internal attention patterns align with phonosemantic relationships?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that MLLMs exhibit phonetic intuitions aligning with linguistic research and that their internal attention patterns highlight focus on iconic phonemes, bridging AI and cognitive linguistics.
papers.conclusion: MLLMs demonstrate phonetic iconicity and internal attention mechanisms that reflect sound symbolism, providing insights into multimodal interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs show phonetic intuition across multiple semantic dimensions, performing above baseline for both natural and constructed words.
Models have modality-specific preferences, using audio for acoustically grounded features and text for articulatory or visually driven features.
There are discrepancies between human and model performance, with models not fully aligning with human semantic alignment.
Attention analysis reveals that MLLMs attend to sound-symbolic phonemes, with higher attention in late layers for constructed words.
The constructed word group shows clearer phonosemantic attention patterns compared to natural words.
papers.limitation:
Discrepancies exist between human phonetic intuition and model performance, indicating models are not fully human-like in semantic alignment.
Models may overlook subtle phonosemantic cues due to training on large-scale distributional semantics of natural languages.
papers.abstract: Sound symbolism is a linguistic concept that refers to non-arbitrary associations between phonetic forms and their meanings. We suggest that this can be a compelling probe into how Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) interpret auditory information in human languages. We investigate MLLMs' performance on phonetic iconicity across textual (orthographic and IPA) and auditory forms of inputs with up to 25 semantic dimensions (e.g., sharp vs. round), observing models' layer-wise information processing by measuring phoneme-level attention fraction scores. To this end, we present LEX-ICON, an extensive mimetic word dataset consisting of 8,052 words from four natural languages (English, French, Japanese, and Korean) and 2,930 systematically constructed pseudo-words, annotated with semantic features applied across both text and audio modalities. Our key findings demonstrate (1) MLLMs' phonetic intuitions that align with existing linguistic research across multiple semantic dimensions and (2) phonosemantic attention patterns that highlight models' focus on iconic phonemes. These results bridge domains of artificial intelligence and cognitive linguistics, providing the first large-scale, quantitative analyses of phonetic iconicity in terms of MLLMs' interpretability.

papers.title: On the Linguistic Representational Power of Neural Machine Translation Models
papers.research_question: How do neural machine translation models capture linguistic information (morphology, syntax, semantics) in their representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that neural machine translation models learn non-trivial linguistic information in their representations, with a hierarchical organization: lower layers capture local, low-level properties (morphology) and higher layers capture global, high-level properties (syntax, semantics).
papers.conclusion: Deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without direct supervision, learn a substantial amount of linguistic information, and the representations are organized in a hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model.
Lexical semantics and non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model.
Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units.
Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.
The target language impacts the kind of information learned by the MT system, with translation into morphologically-poorer languages leading to better source-side word representations.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of deep neural networks in natural language processing and other spheres of artificial intelligence, their interpretability remains a challenge. We analyze the representations learned by neural machine translation (NMT) models at various levels of granularity and evaluate their quality through relevant extrinsic properties. In particular, we seek answers to the following questions: (i) How accurately is word structure captured within the learned representations, which is an important aspect in translating morphologically rich languages? (ii) Do the representations capture long-range dependencies, and effectively handle syntactically divergent languages? (iii) Do the representations capture lexical semantics? We conduct a thorough investigation along several parameters: (i) Which layers in the architecture capture each of these linguistic phenomena; (ii) How does the choice of translation unit (word, character, or subword unit) impact the linguistic properties captured by the underlying representations? (iii) Do the encoder and decoder learn differently and independently? (iv) Do the representations learned by multilingual NMT models capture the same amount of linguistic information as their bilingual counterparts? Our data-driven, quantitative evaluation illuminates important aspects in NMT models and their ability to capture various linguistic phenomena. We show that deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without being provided any direct supervision during the training process, learn a non-trivial amount of linguistic information. Notable findings include the following observations: (i) Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model; (ii) In contrast, lexical semantics or non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model; (iii) Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units; and (iv) Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: How Transformers Get Rich: Approximation and Dynamics Analysis
papers.research_question: How do transformers implement induction heads, both in terms of approximation and learning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides theoretical analysis showing how two-layer transformers can approximate induction heads and characterizes the training dynamics with a sharp transition from n-gram to induction head learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can efficiently implement induction heads through specific roles of submodules, and learning induction heads involves a sharp transition from n-gram mechanisms driven by time-scale separation and component proportions.
papers.key_findings:
Two-layer single-head transformers without FFNs can approximate vanilla induction heads.
Two-layer multi-head transformers without FFNs can approximate generalized induction heads (in-context n-gram).
Two-layer multi-head transformers with FFNs can approximate generalized induction heads with generic similarity functions.
Training dynamics on a mixed target show a sharp transition from 4-gram to induction head, with four phases.
The transition is driven by time-scale separation in self-attention and speed differences due to component proportions.
papers.limitation:
Extending analysis to rotary positional encoding may be nontrivial.
Dynamics analysis is limited to a simple mixed target without FFNs.
future_direction: Extending analysis to rotary positional encoding.
Generalizing dynamics analysis to nonlinear functions with FFNs.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated exceptional in-context learning capabilities, yet the theoretical understanding of the underlying mechanisms remains limited. A recent work (Elhage et al., 2021) identified a ``rich'' in-context mechanism known as induction head, contrasting with ``lazy'' $n$-gram models that overlook long-range dependencies. In this work, we provide both approximation and dynamics analyses of how transformers implement induction heads. In the {\em approximation} analysis, we formalize both standard and generalized induction head mechanisms, and examine how transformers can efficiently implement them, with an emphasis on the distinct role of each transformer submodule. For the {\em dynamics} analysis, we study the training dynamics on a synthetic mixed target, composed of a 4-gram and an in-context 2-gram component. This controlled setting allows us to precisely characterize the entire training process and uncover an {\em abrupt transition} from lazy (4-gram) to rich (induction head) mechanisms as training progresses.

papers.title: The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs struggle to detect arithmetic errors in their own outputs, and what internal mechanisms are responsible for error detection?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs have a structural dissociation between arithmetic computation (in higher layers) and validation (in middle layers), relying on consistency heads for surface-level alignment checks, which explains their difficulty in error detection.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability provides valuable insights into how LLMs detect or fail to detect arithmetic errors, and the validation gap arises from structural dissociation between computation and validation.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for arithmetic error detection are structurally similar across different models.
Error detection is governed by consistency heads—attention heads in lower to middle layers that check surface-level alignment of numerical values.
Arithmetic computation occurs in higher layers, while validation takes place in middle layers, leading to a structural dissociation.
Patching a small subset of consistency heads can control the model's error detection behavior.
Adding latent activations from higher layers to the residual stream in lower layers significantly enhances error detection, closing the validation gap.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to smaller LLMs and basic math word problems.
Circuit discovery may not be complete, i.e., identified circuits might not include all components involved in the task behavior.
future_direction: Study error detection in larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: The ability of large language models (LLMs) to validate their output and identify potential errors is crucial for ensuring robustness and reliability. However, current research indicates that LLMs struggle with self-correction, encountering significant challenges in detecting errors. While studies have explored methods to enhance self-correction in LLMs, relatively little attention has been given to understanding the models' internal mechanisms underlying error detection. In this paper, we present a mechanistic analysis of error detection in LLMs, focusing on simple arithmetic problems. Through circuit analysis, we identify the computational subgraphs responsible for detecting arithmetic errors across four smaller-sized LLMs. Our findings reveal that all models heavily rely on $\textit{consistency heads}$--attention heads that assess surface-level alignment of numerical values in arithmetic solutions. Moreover, we observe that the models' internal arithmetic computation primarily occurs in higher layers, whereas validation takes place in middle layers, before the final arithmetic results are fully encoded. This structural dissociation between arithmetic computation and validation seems to explain why smaller-sized LLMs struggle to detect even simple arithmetic errors.

papers.title: Linguistics and Human Brain: A Perspective of Computational Neuroscience
papers.research_question: How can computational neuroscience bridge the methodological gap between linguistics and neuroscience to elucidate the language-brain relationship?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes interdisciplinary progress from a computational neuroscience perspective, outlining how it formalizes linguistic theories into testable models and uses large language models to advance model-brain alignment for understanding language processing.
papers.conclusion: This work aims to advance a comprehensive, mechanistic understanding of the language-brain relationship and promote computational neuroscience as a generative theoretical framework for testable neuro-computational accounts of language.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal interactions between language and perceptual systems (e.g., vision, music) exist and are partially captured by multimodal large models, providing tools for studying semantic coding.
Inter-brain neural coupling during communication shows alignment between speaker and listener neural systems, with coupling strength increasing with shared semantic representations.
Hierarchical computation in large language models aligns with brain processing, but differences exist, prompting debate on whether models implement genuine hierarchical computation or statistical learning.
Large language models and humans show similar sensitivities in learning strategies, such as in-context learning, revealing parallels in adaptive language processing.
Language plasticity in the brain, including acquisition and adaptation, can be studied through model-brain alignment, offering insights into neural mechanisms of learning and recovery.
papers.limitation:
Functional alignment without structural homology
Constraints on real-time validation
Biased research coverage
Narrow evaluation metrics
future_direction: Improving biological plausibility via spiking neural network–based language models
Developing cognitive-level alignment frameworks integrating memory, causality, and metacognition
Extending clinical applications and brain–computer interface applications
papers.abstract: Elucidating the language-brain relationship requires bridging the methodological gap between the abstract theoretical frameworks of linguistics and the empirical neural data of neuroscience. Serving as an interdisciplinary cornerstone, computational neuroscience formalizes the hierarchical and dynamic structures of language into testable neural models through modeling, simulation, and data analysis. This enables a computational dialogue between linguistic hypotheses and neural mechanisms. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly large language models (LLMs), have powerfully advanced this pursuit. Their high-dimensional representational spaces provide a novel scale for exploring the neural basis of linguistic processing, while the "model-brain alignment" framework offers a methodology to evaluate the biological plausibility of language-related theories.

papers.title: What Do They Capture? -- A Structural Analysis of Pre-Trained Language Models for Source Code
papers.research_question: The paper investigates why pre-trained language models for source code work and what feature correlations they capture, specifically focusing on whether they learn the syntactical structure of source code.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a structural analysis of pre-trained language models for source code, showing that attention aligns with syntax structure, syntax information is embedded in contextual word embeddings, and the models can induce syntax trees to some extent.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that pre-trained code models capture syntactic structure, which may explain their effectiveness and inspire future work on code representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Attention aligns strongly with the syntax structure of code.
Pre-training language models of code can preserve the syntax structure of code in the intermediate representations of each Transformer layer.
The pre-trained models of code have the ability of inducing syntax trees of code.
Attention aligns better with syntax in deeper layers than in lower layers.
Extracting parse trees from attention information is more effective than from contextual representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is based on AST structure only, which is just one aspect of source code.
The structural probing approach is relatively simple and could be improved with a deep neural network.
The tree construction algorithm is simple and the right-skewness bias was designed for natural language, not ASTs.
future_direction: Investigate how pre-trained models learn other aspects of source code (e.g., tokens, control-flow graphs, data-flow graphs).
Extend the analysis to other models (e.g., supervised learning models, LSTM, CNN).
Develop a deep neural network for better mapping in structural probing and improve the tree construction algorithm for ASTs.
papers.abstract: Recently, many pre-trained language models for source code have been proposed to model the context of code and serve as a basis for downstream code intelligence tasks such as code completion, code search, and code summarization. These models leverage masked pre-training and Transformer and have achieved promising results. However, currently there is still little progress regarding interpretability of existing pre-trained code models. It is not clear why these models work and what feature correlations they can capture. In this paper, we conduct a thorough structural analysis aiming to provide an interpretation of pre-trained language models for source code (e.g., CodeBERT, and GraphCodeBERT) from three distinctive perspectives: (1) attention analysis, (2) probing on the word embedding, and (3) syntax tree induction. Through comprehensive analysis, this paper reveals several insightful findings that may inspire future studies: (1) Attention aligns strongly with the syntax structure of code. (2) Pre-training language models of code can preserve the syntax structure of code in the intermediate representations of each Transformer layer. (3) The pre-trained models of code have the ability of inducing syntax trees of code. Theses findings suggest that it may be helpful to incorporate the syntax structure of code into the process of pre-training for better code representations.

papers.title: From Indirect Object Identification to Syllogisms: Exploring Binary Mechanisms in Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small handle binary truth values in syllogistic prompts, and what circuits are responsible for logical reasoning in these tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies circuits in GPT-2 small that handle syllogistic reasoning, uncovering binary mechanisms such as negation via negative attention heads and modulation via MLPs, and shows these circuits achieve high faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: By relating the findings on syllogistic reasoning circuits to prior IOI analysis, the paper provides new insights into the roles of attention heads and MLPs in LLMs, contributing to a broader understanding of model reasoning and future mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Identified three distinct circuits for simple, opposite, and complex syllogisms in GPT-2 small.
Discovered a binary negation mechanism where negative truth heads produce the opposite token, aided by MLPs that rescale the residual stream.
Found empirical evidence for binary opposite tasks, showing the same attention heads flip their influence on logit difference between simple and opposite syllogisms.
Advanced interpretability of model components, detailing the roles of truth heads, negative truth heads, truth modulation heads, induction heads, and duplicate statement identifier heads.
Demonstrated that a circuit comprising three attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model's performance on the simple syllogism task.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) can perform a wide range of tasks, and mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer the components responsible for task completion to understand their behavior. Previous mechanistic interpretability research has primarily focused on linguistic tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI). In this paper, we investigate the ability of GPT-2 small to handle binary truth values by analyzing its behavior with syllogistic prompts, such as "Statement A is true. Statement B matches statement A. Statement B is'', which requires more complex logical reasoning compared to IOI. Through our analysis of several syllogism tasks of varying difficulty, we identify multiple circuits that explain GPT-2 small’s logical-reasoning capabilities and uncover binary mechanisms that facilitate task completion, including the ability to produce a negated token that does not appear in the input prompt through negative heads. Our evaluation using a faithfulness metric shows that a circuit comprising three attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model’s performance. By relating our findings to IOI analysis, we provide new insights into the roles of attention heads and MLPs in LLMs. We believe these insights contribute to a broader understanding of model reasoning and benefit future research in mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
papers.research_question: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? The paper proposes a benchmark to provide a basis for comparisons.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MIB, a benchmark for mechanistic interpretability with two tracks (circuit localization and causal variable localization) to enable meaningful comparisons of interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: MIB provides a standardized benchmark for comparing mechanistic interpretability methods, enabling meaningful evaluations and demonstrating progress in the field.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization.
Supervised Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) performs best on causal variable localization.
Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are not better than non-featurized hidden vectors (neurons) for causal variable localization.
MIB enables meaningful comparisons and shows real progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The set of models and tasks is incomplete, limiting generalizability.
The metrics may not capture all aspects of interpretability that researchers care about.
The benchmark focuses on localization and featurization, leaving out other mechanistic interpretability goals like editing or control.
future_direction: Expand MIB to include more models and tasks.
Develop more comprehensive metrics that capture other aspects of interpretability.
Extend the benchmark to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? In pursuit of lasting evaluation standards, we propose MIB, a Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, with two tracks spanning four tasks and five models. MIB favors methods that precisely and concisely recover relevant causal pathways or causal variables in neural language models. The circuit localization track compares methods that locate the model components - and connections between them - most important for performing a task (e.g., attribution patching or information flow routes). The causal variable localization track compares methods that featurize a hidden vector, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs) or distributed alignment search (DAS), and align those features to a task-relevant causal variable. Using MIB, we find that attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization. For causal variable localization, we find that the supervised DAS method performs best, while SAE features are not better than neurons, i.e., non-featurized hidden vectors. These findings illustrate that MIB enables meaningful comparisons, and increases our confidence that there has been real progress in the field.

papers.title: Unveiling Language Competence Neurons: A Psycholinguistic Approach to Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do language models capture deeper cognitive aspects of language competence, and can specific neurons be identified that correspond to such competence?
papers.core_contribution: The study shows that in GPT-2-XL, human-like language competence in psycholinguistic tasks is supported by specific neurons, as evidenced by ablation and activation experiments; tasks where the model lacks competence show no such neuron specialization.
papers.conclusion: Psycholinguistic tasks offer a powerful framework for probing neuron-level representations in language models, linking language abilities to specific neurons and providing insights into how LLMs process language.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2-XL does not exhibit human-like sound-shape association, and neuron manipulation does not affect performance on this task.
GPT-2-XL shows marginal human-like sound-gender association, and neuron manipulation (ablation and activation) affects performance, indicating specific neurons are involved.
GPT-2-XL shows strong human-like implicit causality understanding, and neuron manipulation strongly affects performance, indicating specific neurons are crucial.
The top 5 and top 50 neurons identified by accumulative direct effect are causally important for tasks where the model exhibits competence.
Psycholinguistic tasks can be used to probe neuron-level representations in language models, linking language abilities to specific neurons.
papers.limitation:
Use of GPT-2-XL, an older and smaller model, which may not generalize to newer models.
Focus on only three psycholinguistic tasks, which provides a narrow view of language competence.
Granularity of neuron manipulation techniques may overlook distributed representations.
future_direction: Extend these methods to more advanced models.
Explore additional psycholinguistic phenomena.
Investigate other LLM architectures.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance in their linguistic capacity, understanding how they capture aspects of language competence remains a significant challenge. This study therefore employs psycholinguistic paradigms in English, which are well-suited for probing deeper cognitive aspects of language processing, to explore neuron-level representations in language model across three tasks: sound-shape association, sound-gender association, and implicit causality. Our findings indicate that while GPT-2-XL struggles with the sound-shape task, it demonstrates human-like abilities in both sound-gender association and implicit causality. Targeted neuron ablation and activation manipulation reveal a crucial relationship: When GPT-2-XL displays a linguistic ability, specific neurons correspond to that competence; conversely, the absence of such an ability indicates a lack of specialized neurons. This study is the first to utilize psycholinguistic experiments to investigate deep language competence at the neuron level, providing a new level of granularity in model interpretability and insights into the internal mechanisms driving language ability in the transformer-based LLM.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and the components of reasoning tasks (knowledge retrieval vs. knowledge-free reasoning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-free reasoning capability transfers nearly perfectly across languages, whereas knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer, attributed to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: The demand for knowledge retrieval significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer performance, while knowledge-free reasoning ability can be nearly fully transferred between languages, due to shared neural mechanisms for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge retrieval component significantly hinders cross-lingual transfer in reasoning tasks; more knowledge retrieval leads to lower transfer effectiveness.
Knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across languages after fine-tuning in one language.
Cross-lingual computational similarity (hidden states and neuron activation) is higher for knowledge-free reasoning than for knowledge retrieval, especially in middle layers.
Target language proficiency impacts transferability; improving proficiency enhances cross-lingual transfer for knowledge-free reasoning.
The model uses similar neurons for knowledge-free reasoning across languages, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited model selection and language coverage, primarily relying on LLaMA-2 and only ten languages.
Depth of interpretability analysis is limited; macro-level numerical analyses without precisely identifying specific neurons.
future_direction: Conduct more detailed neuron-level analyses to verify hypotheses about shared neurons for reasoning and language-specific knowledge storage.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities across multiple languages. However, the relationship between capabilities in different languages is less explored. In this work, we decompose the process of reasoning tasks into two separated components: knowledge retrieval and knowledge-free reasoning, and analyze the relationship between cross-lingual transferability and these two components. With adapted commonsense reasoning datasets and constructed knowledge-free reasoning datasets, we show that the knowledge-free reasoning capability can be nearly perfectly transferred across various source-target language directions despite the secondary impact of resource in some specific target languages, while cross-lingual knowledge retrieval significantly hinders the transfer. Moreover, by analyzing the hidden states and feed-forward network neuron activation during the reasoning, we show that higher similarity of hidden representations and larger overlap of activated neurons could explain the better cross-lingual transferability of knowledge-free reasoning than knowledge retrieval. Thus, we hypothesize that knowledge-free reasoning shares similar neurons in different languages for reasoning, while knowledge is stored separately in different languages. Our code and data is available at: https://github.com/NJUNLP/Knowledge-Free-Reasoning.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models with applications to the financial services industry
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to understand the inner workings of large language models for financial services applications, specifically for compliance monitoring?
papers.core_contribution: This paper pioneers the application of mechanistic interpretability to financial services, designing algorithmic tasks for compliance monitoring and analyzing GPT-2 Small's attention patterns for identifying potential Fair Lending violations.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability techniques can be successfully applied to understand LLM behavior in financial compliance tasks, providing insights into the roles of specific attention heads and MLP layers.
papers.key_findings:
Heads 11.4, 8.9, and 6.3 contribute positively to the Fair Lending task completion, while heads 0.6, 11.0, and 10.7 contribute negatively.
MLP layers 2 and 4 significantly improve task completion, while MLP layer 10 and attention layer 0 decrease performance.
Activation patching reveals that heads 10.2, 10.7, and 11.3 (positive) and heads 9.6 and 10.6 (negative) play significant roles, with head 10.2's value vector being particularly important.
The Fair Lending compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, involving information processing across many layers rather than being localized to a few final layers.
Value patching has a more significant effect than key or query patching for important heads in later layers (9-11).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to GPT-2 Small, a relatively small model, and may not generalize to larger, more powerful LLMs.
The financial compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, making circuit discovery more challenging and less localized.
future_direction: Conducting experiments with more powerful open-source LLMs such as Mistral 7B and Llama-2 7B.
Working on more algorithmic examples of compliance tasks in financial services and finding prompts that result in large logit differences.
Performing path patching as a more sophisticated circuit discovery approach for end-to-end circuit identification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit remarkable capabilities across a broad spectrum of applications. Nevertheless, due to their intrinsic complexity, these models present substantial challenges in interpreting their internal decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses critical challenges when it comes to their adaptation by financial institutions, where concerns and accountability regarding bias, fairness, and reliability are of paramount importance. Mechanistic interpretability aims at reverse engineering complex AI models such as transformers. In this paper, we are pioneering the use of mechanistic interpretability to shed some light on the inner workings of large language models for use in financial services applications. We offer several examples of how algorithmic tasks can be designed for compliance monitoring purposes. In particular, we investigate GPT-2 Small’s attention pattern when prompted to identify potential violation of Fair Lending laws. Using direct logit attribution, we study the contributions of each layer and its corresponding attention heads to the logit difference in the residual stream. Finally, we design clean and corrupted prompts and use activation patching as a causal intervention method to localize our task completion components further. We observe that the (positive) heads 10.2 (head 2, layer 10), 10.7, and 11.3, as well as the (negative) heads 9.6 and 10.6 play a significant role in the task completion.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: Overlap in meaning is a stronger predictor of semantic activation in GPT-3 than in humans
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences in semantic activation patterns between GPT-3 and humans, particularly regarding the role of semantic similarity versus associative similarity?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-3's semantic activation patterns are broadly similar to humans, but semantic similarity is a stronger predictor of activation in GPT-3 than associative similarity, unlike in humans where associative similarity plays a larger role.
papers.conclusion: GPT-3's semantic network is organized more around word meaning than co-occurrence, suggesting differences from human semantic memory, but with similarities that can inform psycholinguistic research.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-3 shows higher semantic activation for first-associate word pairs compared to other-associate and unrelated pairs, similar to humans.
GPT-3's semantic activation is more strongly driven by semantic similarity (e.g., synonyms, antonyms) than by associative similarity (e.g., phrasal associates).
Humans show relatively stronger activation for associatively similar words, while GPT-3 shows stronger activation for semantically similar words.
The importance of semantic similarity in predicting activation increases with model complexity and recency.
Differences in measurement approaches (direct cosine similarity vs. indirect reaction times) may contribute to observed disparities.
papers.limitation: Semantic priming effects in humans measured via lexical decision tasks may be affected by processes like expectancy or semantic matching, introducing noise or bias not present in GPT-3's direct measurement.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models generate texts that are virtually indistinguishable from those written by humans and achieve near-human performance in comprehension and reasoning tests. Yet, their complexity makes it difficult to explain and predict their functioning. We examined a state-of-the-art language model (GPT-3) using lexical decision tasks widely used to study the structure of semantic memory in humans. The results of four analyses showed that GPT-3's patterns of semantic activation are broadly similar to those observed in humans, showing significantly higher semantic activation in related (e.g., "lime-lemon") word pairs than in other-related (e.g., "sour-lemon") or unrelated (e.g., "tourist-lemon") word pairs. However, there are also significant differences between GPT-3 and humans. GPT-3's semantic activation is better predicted by similarity in words' meaning (i.e., semantic similarity) rather than their co-occurrence in the language (i.e., associative similarity). This suggests that GPT-3's semantic network is organized around word meaning rather than their co-occurrence in text.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models? Specifically, are there language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization and discovers two novel types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons, which store knowledge across languages, and degenerate knowledge neurons, which provide functional overlap for robust fact storage and can be used for fact-checking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that their AMIG method enables precise knowledge localization and reveals two types of neurons that provide insights into knowledge storage, with language-independent neurons enabling cross-lingual editing and degenerate neurons enabling fact-checking.
papers.key_findings:
AMIG localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than previous methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons are concentrated in the final one or two layers and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist and can help PLMs detect wrong facts, improving fact-checking performance.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models like BERT and GPT-2.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration of knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Unpacking Robustness in Inflectional Languages: Adversarial Evaluation and Mechanistic Insights
papers.research_question: How do adversarial attacks perform in inflectional languages, and how does inflection affect model robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper evaluates adversarial attacks in inflectional languages and uses a novel mechanistic interpretability protocol based on Edge Attribution Patching to identify inflection-specific circuits, showing these circuits contribute to model robustness.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating inflection in language model training can increase robustness against adversarial attacks, especially those that manipulate characters within words. Mechanistic interpretability successfully identifies inflection-specific circuits that contribute to this resilience.
papers.key_findings:
TextBugger is the most effective attack method but produces lower-quality adversarial examples in terms of similarity metrics.
Models trained on inflectional languages (Polish, Czech) show different robustness patterns compared to English, depending on the task.
Inflection-specific circuits can be identified in Polish models, and these circuits are more robust to adversarial attacks.
The inclusion of inflection-specific components in circuits improves model robustness against adversarial perturbations.
The Natural Language Inference (NLI) similarity metric shows high variance and may not be reliable for evaluating adversarial example quality.
papers.limitation:
Limited availability of high-quality annotated datasets for less widely studied languages, such as Czech.
High cost and labor intensity of producing parallel datasets for circuit discovery, requiring accurate tokenization and linguistic expertise.
future_direction: Investigate additional dimensions of model robustness with attention to the structural and functional properties of internal model circuits.
Assess the resilience of identified circuits to adversarial perturbations.
Address the challenge of creating high-quality datasets specifically tailored for circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Various techniques are used in the generation of adversarial examples, including methods such as TextBugger which introduce minor, hardly visible perturbations to words leading to changes in model behaviour. Another class of techniques involves substituting words with their synonyms in a way that preserves the text's meaning but alters its predicted class, with TextFooler being a prominent example of such attacks. Most adversarial example generation methods are developed and evaluated primarily on non-inflectional languages, typically English. In this work, we evaluate and explain how adversarial attacks perform in inflectional languages. To explain the impact of inflection on model behaviour and its robustness under attack, we designed a novel protocol inspired by mechanistic interpretability, based on Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) method. The proposed evaluation protocol relies on parallel task-specific corpora that include both inflected and syncretic variants of texts in two languages -- Polish and English. To analyse the models and explain the relationship between inflection and adversarial robustness, we create a new benchmark based on task-oriented dataset MultiEmo, enabling the identification of mechanistic inflection-related elements of circuits within the model and analyse their behaviour under attack.

papers.title: BlackboxNLP-2025 MIB Shared Task: Improving Circuit Faithfulness via Better Edge Selection
papers.research_question: How to improve circuit faithfulness via better edge selection in circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes bootstrapping, positive-negative ratio (PNR), and integer linear programming (ILP) for edge selection in circuit discovery, improving faithfulness over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Principled edge selection improves faithfulness and enables more robust circuit discovery, despite computational limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Bootstrapping identifies edges with consistent attribution scores, filtering out unstable ones.
Positive-negative ratio (PNR) selection balances positive and negative edges, improving circuit faithfulness.
Integer linear programming (ILP) provides globally optimal edge selection compared to greedy algorithms.
Combinations of these methods outperform baseline approaches across multiple models and tasks on MIB metrics.
papers.limitation:
ILP optimization scales poorly with edge count, limiting applicability to larger models.
Optimal ratio of positive edges varies by models and tasks, requiring task-specific tuning.
Gap between state-of-the-art attribution methods and 'ground truth' edge importance scores limits faithfulness gains from ILP.
papers.abstract: One of the main challenges in mechanistic interpretability is circuit discovery, determining which parts of a model perform a given task. We build on the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (MIB) and propose three key improvements to circuit discovery. First, we use bootstrapping to identify edges with consistent attribution scores. Second, we introduce a simple ratio-based selection strategy to prioritize strong positive-scoring edges, balancing performance and faithfulness. Third, we replace the standard greedy selection with an integer linear programming formulation. Our methods yield more faithful circuits and outperform prior approaches across multiple MIB tasks and models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/MIB-Shared-Task.

papers.title: The Computational Complexity of Circuit Discovery for Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the computational complexity of circuit discovery queries for inner interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a complexity analysis of circuit discovery queries, showing that many are intractable (NP-hard, Σp2-hard, etc.), but also identifies tractable relaxations such as quasi-minimal circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuit discovery for inner interpretability is computationally challenging, but identifies tractable relaxations and provides a framework for understanding the complexity of interpretability queries.
papers.key_findings:
Many circuit discovery queries (e.g., sufficient circuit, circuit ablation) are NP-hard or Σp2-hard.
Some queries remain fixed-parameter intractable (W[1]-hard) even when parameterizing by model depth or other features.
Some queries are inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes.
There is a formal separation between local and global query complexity, which helps explain interpretability illusions.
Quasi-minimal circuit queries are tractable (PTIME) and retain useful affordances for description and control.
future_direction: Empirical and formal characterization of learned weights to inform average-case analyses.
Exploring more parameters for fixed-parameter tractability in circuit discovery queries.
Designing queries that rely on mid-level abstractions to bridge circuits and human-intelligible algorithms.
papers.abstract: Many proposed applications of neural networks in machine learning, cognitive/brain science, and society hinge on the feasibility of inner interpretability via circuit discovery. This calls for empirical and theoretical explorations of viable algorithmic options. Despite advances in the design and testing of heuristics, there are concerns about their scalability and faithfulness at a time when we lack understanding of the complexity properties of the problems they are deployed to solve. To address this, we study circuit discovery with classical and parameterized computational complexity theory: (1) we describe a conceptual scaffolding to reason about circuit finding queries in terms of affordances for description, explanation, prediction and control; (2) we formalize a comprehensive set of queries for mechanistic explanation, and propose a formal framework for their analysis; (3) we use it to settle the complexity of many query variants and relaxations of practical interest on multi-layer perceptrons. Our findings reveal a challenging complexity landscape. Many queries are intractable, remain fixed-parameter intractable relative to model/circuit features, and inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes. To navigate this landscape, we prove there exist transformations to tackle some of these hard problems with better-understood heuristics, and prove the tractability or fixed-parameter tractability of more modest queries which retain useful affordances. This framework allows us to understand the scope and limits of interpretability queries, explore viable options, and compare their resource demands on existing and future architectures.

papers.title: Does BERT Understand Idioms? A Probing-Based Empirical Study of BERT Encodings of Idioms
papers.research_question: Can BERT distinguish the idiomatic usage of a potentially idiomatic expression (PIE) from its literal usage? Can BERT understand the idiomatic meaning of an idiom?
papers.core_contribution: BERT can distinguish literal and idiomatic usages of potentially idiomatic expressions with high accuracy and encodes idiomatic meaning to some extent, but contextualization affects paraphrase identification differently for idioms and general multi-word expressions.
papers.conclusion: BERT is able to detect idiomatic usages of potentially idiomatic expressions with high accuracy and encode idiomatic meaning to some extent, but the effect of contextualization for multi-word expressions and idioms requires further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
BERT can separate literal and idiomatic usages of potentially idiomatic expressions with high accuracy (around 90%).
BERT can encode the idiomatic meaning of idioms to some extent, as shown by paraphrase identification performance above random baseline.
Contextualization in BERT helps most in recognizing literal usages of PIEs.
For paraphrase identification, contextualization hurts performance for general multi-word expressions but not for idioms.
The model's classification errors tend to occur on instances with lower human annotation agreement.
future_direction: Further exploration to fully explain the different effects of contextualization for multi-word expressions and idioms.
papers.abstract: Understanding idioms is important in NLP. In this paper, we study to what extent a pretrained BERT model is able to encode the meaning of a potentially idiomatic expression (PIE) in a certain context. We make use of a few existing datasets and perform two probing tasks: PIE usage classification and idiom paraphrase identification. Our experiment results suggest that BERT indeed is able to separate the literal and idiomatic usages of a PIE with high accuracy. It is also able to encode the idiomatic meaning of a PIE to some extent.

papers.title: Contextual modulation of language comprehension in a dynamic neural model of lexical meaning
papers.research_question: How does contextual modulation affect lexical meaning comprehension in a dynamic neural model? The paper investigates the semantic basis of lexical polysemy using the English word 'have' as a test case.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a dynamic neural model of lexical meaning that explains contextual modulation in language comprehension, showing that polysemy arises from transiently stable neural activation states on continuous semantic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that lexical polysemy is best explained by continuous neural dynamics on semantic dimensions, rather than by discrete meaning representations.
papers.key_findings:
Model simulations capture contextual modulation of lexical semantic interpretation and individual variation in this modulation.
Simulations generate a novel prediction that the relationship between sentence reading time and acceptability should be contextually modulated.
The behavioral experiment replicates previous results showing higher acceptability and faster reading times for sentences in an adjacency context.
The experiment partially confirms the model's novel prediction regarding the interaction between context and acceptability in reading time.
Individual variation in contextual facilitation is correlated with Autism-Spectrum Quotient scores, supporting the model's account of individual differences.
future_direction: Extend the model to other polysemous words and interpretations beyond the English word 'have'.
papers.abstract: We computationally implement and experimentally test the behavioral predictions of a dynamic neural model of lexical meaning in the framework of Dynamic Field Theory. We demonstrate the architecture and behavior of the model using as a test case the English lexical item have, focusing on its polysemous use. In the model, have maps to a semantic space defined by two independently motivated continuous conceptual dimensions, connectedness and control asymmetry. The mapping is modeled as coupling between a neural node representing the lexical item and neural fields representing the conceptual dimensions. While lexical knowledge is modeled as a stable coupling pattern, real-time lexical meaning retrieval is modeled as the motion of neural activation patterns between transiently stable states corresponding to semantic interpretations or readings. Model simulations capture two previously reported empirical observations: (1) contextual modulation of lexical semantic interpretation, and (2) individual variation in the magnitude of this modulation. Simulations also generate a novel prediction that the by-trial relationship between sentence reading time and acceptability should be contextually modulated. An experiment combining self-paced reading and acceptability judgments replicates previous results and partially bears out the model's novel prediction. Altogether, results support a novel perspective on lexical polysemy: that the many related meanings of a word are not categorically distinct representations; rather, they are transiently stable neural activation states that arise from the nonlinear dynamics of neural populations governing interpretation on continuous semantic dimensions. Our model offers important advantages over related models in the dynamical systems framework, as well as models based on Bayesian inference.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success.
